findings.statement: Porting SkellyCam's ring buffer to C++ without changing the algorithm gains only 2-7%: the cost of put_frame is the algorithm (fresh allocation + 2 copies), not the language.
findings.evidence: cpp/results/cpp_comparison.md 1a: ring_write/write_1080p_n1_sk_head.json 1.326 ms vs write_1080p_n1_cpp_head_port.json 1.276 ms; write_1080p_n5_sk_head(_r2) 2.765/2.780 vs cpp_head_port(_r2) 2.694/2.662 ms; 720p 0.614 vs 0.574 and 1.140/1.157 vs 1.121/1.117 ms. Code: https://github.com/freemocap/skellycam/blob/23ccbf208e43879bfc74fc01049e5af2a623933d/skellycam/core/ipc/shared_memory/ring_buffer_shared_memory.py#L118-L133. Scripts: py_ring.py write <size> <n> sk_head 10; ringbench.exe write <size> <n> head_port 10 (run_matrix.py ring_write).

findings.statement: With the same one-copy seqlock design, Python (numpy), the pybind11 hybrid, ctypes and pure C++ write frames at the same speed (within ~1-4%), and Python gets the full 4.4-9x gain of removing the extra copy.
findings.evidence: ring_write: 1080p N=1 py_seq 0.1466 / hybrid 0.1465 / hybrid_ctypes 0.1466 / cpp_one_copy 0.1456 ms; N=5 0.635/0.635, 0.621/0.613, 0.654/0.621, 0.637/0.630 ms; vs sk_head 1.326 (N=1) and 2.765 (N=5) ms. Script: run_matrix.py ring_write.

findings.statement: For a lossless writer->reader pipeline across processes, C++ sustains the same throughput as the numpy seqlock ring at frame sizes; both sustain about 2.2x SkellyCam HEAD's ring and about 9x the 60 fps target at 5x1080p. Paced 5x60 is met by every implementation with 0 lost and 0 torn frames.
findings.evidence: ring_spsc/spsc_1080p_n5_max_*.json: slowest-camera 543/535 (cpp_proc), 545/545 (cpp_thread), 530/526 (hybrid), 527/537 (py_seq), 243/250 (sk_head) fps; 720p 1256-1288 vs 603. spsc_*_paced60_*: 3000/3000 read, 0 lost, 0 torn; publish->read median 1.945 (cpp_proc) vs 2.019 (py_seq) vs 3.736 (sk_head) ms at 1080p. 50 SPSC runs, 0 lost / 0 torn / 0 seq rejects (cpp_comparison.json ring_spsc). Script: run_matrix.py ring_spsc.

findings.statement: Bulk copy bandwidth is the shared hardware ceiling: numpy np.copyto and MSVC memcpy are within 1-5% at 720p/1080p, single- and multi-threaded, and AVX2 streaming stores add at most ~3% at frame sizes.
findings.evidence: memcpy_cpp.json vs memcpy_py.json: 1080p hot->ring 42.37 (memcpy) / 43.69 (nt) / 41.23 (np.copyto) / 40.72 (slot assign) GB/s; cold->cold 17.75/17.54/17.42; 2 threads 53.6/55.3/55.0; 8 threads 40.2/40.7/40.0. Scripts: memcpybench.exe, py_memcpy.py.

findings.statement: C++ wins clearly only on per-call fixed overhead, which shows with tiny frames and is irrelevant at 5x60: a 64x64 publish costs 0.8 us in C++, 1.4 us in lean numpy and 24.8 us in SkellyCam HEAD; the SPSC rate at 64x64 (1 pair) is 3.3x higher in C++ than lean Python.
findings.evidence: ring_write/write_64x64_n1_*.json; ring_spsc/spsc_64x64_n1_max_*.json: 1,149,700 (cpp_proc) vs 347,056 (py_seq) vs 12,977 (sk_head) fps. At 300 frames/s, 0.6 us/frame is ~0.18 ms of CPU per second (arithmetic).

findings.statement: SkellyCam's per-frame control-plane overhead is a Python-wrapper problem fixable in Python: SharedMemoryNumber.value costs 4.4-5.7 us and a nested recarray timestamp write 13.5 us, against 54-60 ns for a numpy view (C++ atomic 0.2-0.3 ns).
findings.evidence: micro_py.json rows skellycam_SharedMemoryNumber_value_write/read 4,423/5,738 ns, skellycam_nested_recarray_timestamp_write 13,502 ns, cached_field_view_timestamp_write 53.85 ns, numpy_int64_view_store/load 52.85/60.36 ns; micro_cpp.json atomic 0.18/0.29 ns. Code: https://github.com/freemocap/skellycam/blob/23ccbf208e43879bfc74fc01049e5af2a623933d/skellycam/core/ipc/shared_memory/shared_memory_number.py#L23-L33 and https://github.com/freemocap/skellycam/blob/23ccbf208e43879bfc74fc01049e5af2a623933d/skellycam/core/camera/opencv/opencv_camera_loop.py#L133-L147.

findings.statement: Decode and encode speed is set by the OpenCV / libjpeg-turbo build, not the language: with the same OpenCV version C++ and Python are within ~11%, while Python's cv2 4.12 (libjpeg-turbo 3.1.0) decodes 1.57x and encodes q90 4.9x faster than the C++ OpenCV 4.8 SDK. A C++ port linked against a stock SDK could be slower than today's Python.
findings.evidence: codec/decode_1080p_n1_cpp48_copy.json 11.32 ms, decode_1080p_n1_py48.json 12.78, decode_1080p_n1_py412.json 7.22; imencode_1080p_{cpp48,py48,py412}.json q90 20.00 / 21.19 / 4.11 ms; build info results/opencv_buildinfo_{cpp_sdk_4.8.0,python_4.8.0,python_4.12.0}.txt (JPEG: build-libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3-62 / 2.1.3-62 / 3.1.0-70).

findings.statement: The C++ API can decode straight into a shared-memory slot (cv::imdecode with dst), saving 0.95 ms per 1080p frame (8%); OpenCV 4.12's Python imdecode has no dst, but Python already has in-place alternatives (retrieve(image=slot), simplejpeg into the slot).
findings.evidence: codec/decode_1080p_n1_cpp48_inplace.json 10.36 ms (inplace_ok true) vs decode_1080p_n1_cpp48_copy.json 11.32 ms; 720p 4.62 vs 5.11 ms. Python in-place paths: prototypes/results/p1_write.md rows cur_vcap_into_sk_slot and p_simplejpeg_into_slot.

findings.statement: Recording through cv2.VideoWriter('X264') is the same native MSMF encoder from C++ and Python: identical write latency, encode rate and bitrate. The default-thread-pool CPU blow-up seen in prototypes P10 reproduces in C++, so it is OpenCV behaviour, not a Python cost.
findings.evidence: codec/vw_1080p_n1_max_thdefault_{cpp48,py48,py412}.json: write median 0.699/0.722/0.695 ms, 408.6/408.1/408.8 fps, 125.2 Mbit/s; vw_1080p_n5_paced60_thdefault_*: CPU 1127/1257/1279 %, th1: 382/397/443 %, 0 late writes, frames in file == written. Call matches https://github.com/freemocap/skellycam/blob/23ccbf208e43879bfc74fc01049e5af2a623933d/skellycam/core/recorders/videos/video_recorder.py#L125-L130.

findings.statement: One process with a thread per camera gives no throughput gain over process-per-camera for the ring in C++ (hypothesis C5 refuted for the ring).

The openpnp-style per-pixel BGR->RGB swap + flip is 7.7x slower as a numpy strided copy than as a C++ loop, but calling OpenCV's cvtColor + flip from Python is faster still (0.443 vs 0.743 ms at 1080p), so C2 is not an argument for C++.
findings.evidence: memcpy_cpp.json pixel_op swap_bgr_rgb_and_flip_loop 0.743 ms (1080p); memcpy_py.json swap_bgr_rgb_and_flip 5.736 ms; pixel_cv2_py.json cv2_cvtColor_BGR2RGB_then_flip0 0.443 ms.

findings.statement: Sleep granularity is an OS limit shared by both languages: a 10 us sleep takes ~0.51-0.53 ms either way; naive C++ sleeps (Sleep(1), sleep_for) are worse at ~2.0 ms.
findings.evidence: micro_cpp.json hr_waitable_timer(10us) 513.9 us median; micro_py.json time.sleep(1e-05) 525.4 us; Sleep(1) 2000.0 us, this_thread::sleep_for(10us) 2007.8 us. SkellyCam polls with time.sleep(1e-5): https://github.com/freemocap/skellycam/blob/23ccbf208e43879bfc74fc01049e5af2a623933d/skellycam/utilities/wait_functions.py#L29-L30.

findings.statement: VERDICT: a C++ port is not needed to reach 5 cameras x 60 fps and would not raise throughput meaningfully; the Python fixes (remove copy.copy, one-copy seqlock ring, cached views, decoupled recorder, decode into the slot) capture essentially all the gain. EXTRAPOLATION: in the baseline 1080p mjpeg loop (retrieve ~10.1-10.3, put_frame ~3.6-3.7, record ~1.1-1.2 ms) a line-by-line C++ port would save ~0.1 ms of put_frame and nothing on retrieve/record; the Python fixes save ~2.1 ms of put (2.77 -> 0.64 ms at 5x1080p isolated) and ~0.42 ms of control-plane writes.
findings.evidence: Component rows above (ring_write 1080p N=5; micro nested timestamp 13.5 us x ~31 writes per frame, count from research.json); baseline/results/e_e2e_summary.md (53.56/53.57 fps; per_camera retrieve/put/record); prototypes/results/p8_e2e_summary.md (Python-only redesign 59.95 fps, 0 never grabbed). Loop: https://github.com/freemocap/skellycam/blob/23ccbf208e43879bfc74fc01049e5af2a623933d/skellycam/core/camera/opencv/opencv_camera_loop.py#L67-L117.

findings.statement: The hybrid option (C++ ring called from Python) works with zero copies across the binding and matches pure C++ at frame sizes; pybind11 and ctypes cost the same per call (~0.5 us more than C++ at 64x64). It is available if portable memory ordering (non-x86) is ever needed.
findings.evidence: ring_write/write_1080p_n1_hybrid.json 0.1465 ms, write_1080p_n1_hybrid_ctypes.json 0.1466 ms vs write_1080p_n1_cpp_one_copy.json 0.1456 ms; 64x64 1.3 / 1.4 / 0.8 us; ring_spsc hybrid 530/526 fps at 5x1080p. Module: cpp/src/cppring_py.cpp (py::buffer, gil_scoped_release).

limitations: Synthetic frames only; no real-camera run in this stage and no native DirectShow/MF capture filter was built, so hypothesis C1 (removing OpenCV's internal SampleCB / getPixels copies) is untested; its upper bound is ~0.07-0.35 ms per removed copy (memcpy rows).
Hypothesis C4 (SEC_LARGE_PAGES) could not be measured: the account lacks SeLockMemoryPrivilege (errors 1300 / 1314), and granting it is a machine-policy change outside this stage.

Only an OpenCV 4.8.0 C++ SDK was available (no C++ OpenCV 4.12, FFmpeg or libjpeg-turbo SDK). Language vs library was separated with a throw-away cv2 4.8.0.76 venv, but the two 4.8.0 builds differ (SDK MSVC 1928 /MD vs wheel MSVC 1900 /MT), so the ~11% decode difference between them is not attributable to the language (open question).
The numpy seqlock (py_seq) relies on x86-64 store ordering; 0 torn frames in 50 SPSC runs is evidence, not proof. The C++ ring uses std::atomic acquire/release.
All readers and blocked writers poll with Sleep(0) (same policy in both languages), so paced-run CPU is dominated by polling and is not a language comparison; event-based wake-up was not measured.
QPC / perf_counter_ns tick is 100 ns: sub-microsecond latencies (ping-pong, 64x64 copies) are quantised; the ns/op values come from throughput loops.
MSMF encoder CPU with OpenCV's default thread pool varies ~10% between runs (1127-1279%); the C++ vs Python CPU differences in those rows are within that spread.
The full end-to-end camera loop was not ported to C++; its effect on the 5x60 e2e result is EXTRAPOLATED from component rows. Disk throughput (N8) was not measured here.

The throw-away cv2 4.8 venv's size was measured but not recorded before deletion (the recording command failed); the 310 codec input files totalled 2,812,836,587 B (results/codec_inputs_manifest.json) and were deleted.
Single machine (i7-14700K, DDR5-4000, Windows 11); thread placement on P/E cores was not pinned.
